D-001.summary: Position VIBE as the methodology and vibestart as the optional bootstrap/runtime product.

context.problem: The product story risked collapsing methodology and bootstrap into one indistinct system.
context.constraints: VIBE must stay agent-agnostic, and vibestart must help rather than become a mandatory prerequisite.

option-1.name: Single indistinct product
option-1.description: Use one name and one surface for both the methodology and the bootstrap product.
option-1.cons: Blurs boundaries and makes adoption look more mandatory than intended.

option-2.name: Separate methodology and product
option-2.description: Treat VIBE as the framework and vibestart as the optional product that installs and operates it.
option-2.pros: Preserves agent-agnostic adoption and creates a cleaner product boundary.

decision.rationale: It protects the framework identity while still allowing vibestart to accelerate adoption.

consequences.positive: Users can adopt VIBE directly or via vibestart.
consequences.negative: Documentation must explain the split clearly.

review.notes: Foundational boundary for all subsequent work.

D-002.summary: Use knowledge-graph.xml as the primary knowledge spine and reject docs/specs as a mandatory side-bridge.

context.problem: Separate narrative specs would create another knowledge surface that agents and humans would need to keep synchronized.
context.constraints: The system must remain graph-first, drift-resistant, and low-noise.

option-1.name: Graph plus mandatory side-doc specs
option-1.description: Keep a human-readable docs/specs bridge between ideas and the canonical XML surfaces.
option-1.cons: Creates a third place to update and accelerates drift.

option-2.name: Graph-first canonical model
option-2.description: Capture ideas first in the graph and project them into requirements, plan, verification, and decisions.
option-2.pros: One semantic spine and fewer synchronization burdens.

decision.rationale: Ideas are already project knowledge; they should enter the knowledge graph immediately and evolve there.

consequences.positive: requirements.xml stays cleaner and more stable.
consequences.negative: The graph ontology must carry more semantic load.

review.notes: Central architectural decision for the framework.

D-003.summary: Keep active manifest in vibe.toml, detailed policy in docs/vibe/*.toml, and runtime exhaust in .vibestart/state.

context.problem: Putting active config, detailed policy, and runtime state in one place would make the system unreadable and hard to review.
context.constraints: Configuration must be inspectable, heavily commented, and agent-agnostic where possible.

option-1.name: One huge root manifest
option-1.description: Put all policy, thresholds, macros, and runtime knobs into vibe.toml.
option-1.cons: Becomes a noisy dump and hard to maintain.

option-2.name: Layered config boundary
option-2.description: Keep root manifest small, detailed policy in docs/vibe, and runtime state isolated under .vibestart/state.
option-2.pros: Readable and reviewable configuration without mixing in operational noise.
option-2.cons: Requires careful documentation of where each setting belongs.

decision.rationale: This keeps config as documentation while protecting the runtime contour from becoming canonical.

consequences.positive: Configuration stays readable and operational noise stays isolated.
consequences.negative: Maintainers must enforce the boundary consistently.

review.notes: Pairs directly with the Config as Documentation principle.

D-004.summary: Define macros as the public API of VIBE and skills as the lower-level implementation operators.

context.problem: Without a stable macro layer, the methodology would be hard to operate and hard to review as an engineering system.
context.constraints: Compatibility must be semantic, not just command-name preservation.

option-1.name: Expose old skills directly
option-1.description: Keep legacy skills as the primary public language.
option-1.cons: Leaks implementation details and preserves old conceptual fragmentation.

option-2.name: Macro-first public API
option-2.description: Use discover, refine, deliver, fix, sync, resume, deploy, vibe, and calibrate as the stable public surface.
option-2.pros: Cleaner orchestration language and better intent-level UX.
option-2.cons: Requires a formal mapping from prior systems.

decision.rationale: Macros are the human-facing contracts; skills remain implementation units that may evolve.

consequences.positive: The framework gets a stable workflow language.
consequences.negative: Compatibility must be documented through lineage and mapping.

review.notes: Needed to make the methodology operable as a real system.

D-005.summary: Make implicit vibe enabled by default and keep guided/single as the safer starting defaults.

context.problem: Users should not have to memorize macro prefixes just to get the methodology benefits, but the system still needs safe execution defaults.
context.constraints: Implicit routing must not remove explicit user control.

option-1.name: Explicit-only routing
option-1.description: Require explicit macro invocations for most interactions.
option-1.cons: Higher cognitive overhead and weaker default UX.

option-2.name: Implicit vibe with safe defaults
option-2.description: Route normal engineering requests through vibe while keeping guided and single as the default execution posture.
option-2.pros: Strong default UX with explicit override paths.
option-2.cons: Requires careful route explanation in guided mode.

decision.rationale: This keeps the system easy to use while preserving a reviewable and explainable execution path.

consequences.positive: Users get VIBE behavior by default instead of manually assembling it.
consequences.negative: Route selection must be transparent in guided mode.

review.notes: Supports the mixed-audience product goal without dumbing down the framework.

D-006.summary: Base adaptive governance on risk and evidence, not on elapsed time, and expose calibration through an explicit expert macro.

context.problem: Agentic work compresses time so aggressively that time-based ritual is a weak proxy for risk.
context.constraints: Policy must stay explainable and tunable through configuration.

option-1.name: Time-heavy governance
option-1.description: Use elapsed time as a major trigger for review and sync.
option-1.cons: Misreads modern agentic throughput and creates bad rituals.

option-2.name: Risk-and-evidence governance with calibration
option-2.description: Use scope, structural change, drift, verification gaps, and review history as the main signals, with explicit policy calibration.
option-2.pros: Better aligned with real engineering risk and easier to tune per project.

decision.rationale: It matches the reality of agentic work and keeps governance inspectable instead of mystical.

consequences.positive: Review and sync become better matched to real risk.
consequences.negative: Thresholds need real-world tuning over time.

review.notes: Calibration is allowed only through explicit analyze, suggest, and apply flows.

D-007.summary: Prioritize a deterministic kernel before expanding autonomous runtime behavior.

context.problem: The draft promised anti-drift and predictability, but routing, projection, and governance semantics were still partly heuristic.
context.constraints: The framework must reduce methodological entropy before it scales autonomy.

option-1.name: Expand runtime surfaces first
option-1.description: Keep broad automation paths and harden the semantics later.
option-1.cons: Lets hidden control drift accumulate in the core.

option-2.name: Deterministic kernel first
option-2.description: Lock projection, routing, and governance algebra before treating aggressive automation as normative.
option-2.pros: Protects the anti-drift and predictability claims at the architectural root.

decision.rationale: VIBE should not claim control-theoretic stability while leaving its core transitions heuristic.

consequences.positive: The framework core becomes reproducible across compliant runtimes.
consequences.negative: Some autonomous flows remain intentionally conservative for longer.

review.notes: Adopted after the first drift-focused audit of the draft.

D-008.summary: Formalize projection and routing as explicit contracts with guards, precedence, and conflict policy.

context.problem: Projection and route selection were explained narratively but not specified strongly enough for deterministic replay.
context.constraints: Graph-first continuity and implicit vibe must stay explainable.

option-1.name: Narrative semantics only
option-1.description: Leave projection and routing mostly descriptive and trust runtime implementations to align.
option-1.cons: High risk of shell-specific drift and inconsistent control flow.

option-2.name: Formal control contracts
option-2.description: Define deterministic routing guards, projection entry stages, idempotence, and conflict precedence.
option-2.cons: Requires more explicit configuration and verification.

decision.rationale: Graph-first systems drift unless the control edges between artifacts and macros are explicit.

consequences.positive: Projection and routing become reproducible and testable.
consequences.negative: The macro/config surface becomes more formal and therefore more verbose.

review.notes: Necessary to keep implicit vibe from becoming hidden control flow.

D-009.summary: Split sync into canonical reconcile and owned-only cleanup phases.

context.problem: One overloaded sync operation would mix canonical mutation and housekeeping with different safety requirements.
context.constraints: sync must remain able to reduce drift without silently deleting or mutating unknown artifacts.

option-1.name: Single combined sync
option-1.description: Use one sync macro to reconcile artifacts and clean operational clutter in one undifferentiated step.
option-1.cons: High ambiguity, weaker safety model, and harder verification.

option-2.name: Two-phase sync
option-2.description: Run reconcile first for canonical surfaces, then optional cleanup only for VIBE-owned operational artifacts.
option-2.pros: Clearer invariants, safer cleanup, and better drift analysis.
option-2.cons: Requires more explicit policy and trace structure.

decision.rationale: Canonical correction and operational cleanup are not the same transaction and should not share the same safety assumptions.

consequences.positive: sync becomes safer and easier to reason about.
consequences.negative: The policy surface must now describe both phases explicitly.

review.notes: Applies both to drift control and to cleanup of operational exhaust.

D-010.summary: Keep guided and single as normative defaults; treat auto, multi, and calibrate apply as experimental until guards mature.

context.problem: The draft already exposed aggressive runtime surfaces before the deterministic kernel and verification model were fully defined.
context.constraints: Experimental does not mean forbidden, but it must not masquerade as the safe baseline.

option-1.name: Normative autonomy by ambition
option-1.description: Default the most convenient macros to auto and rely on later governance hardening.
option-1.cons: Autonomy outpaces proof of safety and increases hidden drift risk.

option-2.name: Conservative normative defaults
option-2.description: Keep guided/single as the baseline and mark auto, multi, and policy mutation as experimental until guarded.
option-2.pros: Matches the stated emphasis on predictability and contract-first control.
option-2.cons: Some users will perceive the framework as more conservative at first.

decision.rationale: Normative defaults should represent the safest proven operating posture, not the most ambitious future posture.

consequences.positive: Framework promises and baseline behavior stay aligned.
consequences.negative: Auto and multi remain opt-in or profile-specific until the kernel matures.

review.notes: Experimental runtime paths remain allowed, but not normative.

D-011.summary: Define vibestart core and deep as product profiles over one methodology.

context.problem: Profile naming could easily drift into a false impression that core and deep are separate framework variants.
context.constraints: VIBE must remain one methodology, while vibestart can expose more than one product depth.

option-1.name: Profiles as methodology variants
option-1.description: Treat core and deep as different framework modes with distinct semantics.
option-1.cons: Breaks methodological coherence and confuses migration.

option-2.name: Profiles as product depth
option-2.description: Treat core and deep as installation and operating-depth profiles over one VIBE methodology.
option-2.pros: Preserves one framework while still allowing different product surfaces.

decision.rationale: It keeps framework semantics stable while allowing vibestart to scale from minimal to richer setup.

consequences.negative: Product docs must explain the difference between methodology and profile depth clearly.

review.notes: Locks the product segmentation without splitting the methodology.

D-012.summary: Require a deterministic first-run contract for vibestart.

context.problem: Without explicit onboarding and first-run behavior, the product would reintroduce hidden defaults and startup ambiguity.
context.constraints: The first-run contract must explain the installed surfaces, defaults, optionals, and next-step behavior.

option-1.name: Minimal install without explicit first-run contract
option-1.description: Install files and let the user infer the product behavior from the repository state.
option-1.cons: Recreates onboarding ambiguity and hidden control flow.

option-2.name: Deterministic first-run contract
option-2.description: State what was installed, what defaults are active, what remains optional, and what happens next.
option-2.pros: Lower startup entropy and stronger operator trust.

decision.rationale: Bootstrap tooling should reduce ambiguity, not relocate it into runtime behavior.

consequences.positive: Operators know exactly what changed and what the next interaction model is.
consequences.negative: Product docs and onboarding messages must stay synchronized.

review.notes: Also constrains recommendation confirmation and implicit routing explanation.

D-013.summary: Keep canonical contract markup and structural labels in English.

context.problem: Locale-dependent contract markup would reduce interoperability across agents, shells, and review tooling.
context.constraints: Human-facing prose may vary by audience, but canonical structural markup must stay stable.

option-1.name: Localized markup
option-1.description: Translate contract labels and structural keys along with explanatory prose.
option-1.pros: Feels more local to one audience.
option-1.cons: Breaks consistency across tools, agents, and migration docs.

option-2.name: English-only contract markup
option-2.description: Keep canonical contract markup and structural labels in English while allowing localized surrounding prose.
option-2.pros: Stable cross-runtime semantics and easier tooling interoperability.
option-2.cons: Requires discipline when writing new canonical surfaces.

decision.rationale: Contract structure is part of the machine-readable and agent-readable protocol surface, not only reader-facing prose.

consequences.positive: Contracts remain portable and easier to validate across tools.
consequences.negative: Writers must separate localized explanation from canonical structure.

review.notes: Applies to contract markup, structural labels, and canonical config keys.

D-014.summary: Allow docs/technology.xml only as a GRACE compatibility shim, not as a new VIBE core artifact.

context.problem: GRACE planning workflows require docs/technology.xml, but VIBE core intentionally does not treat technology.xml as part of its canonical artifact set.
context.constraints: The file may exist for tool compatibility, but it must not compete with the canonical VIBE core surfaces or redefine framework semantics.

option-1.name: Reintroduce technology.xml as a VIBE core artifact
option-1.description: Treat docs/technology.xml as a first-class canonical VIBE surface again.
option-1.pros: Closer alignment with older GRACE tooling assumptions.
option-1.cons: Reopens core artifact scope and weakens the current VIBE boundary design.

option-2.name: Use technology.xml as a compatibility shim only
option-2.description: Keep docs/technology.xml narrowly scoped to GRACE-compatible tooling while preserving the current VIBE core artifact model.
option-2.pros: Unlocks GRACE planning flows without changing VIBE core semantics.
option-2.cons: Requires explicit documentation so the shim is not mistaken for a new source of truth.

decision.chosen: Use technology.xml as a compatibility shim only
decision.rationale: Compatibility should unblock reuse of proven GRACE workflows without silently expanding the VIBE core surface area.

consequences.positive: GRACE-compatible planning tools can run without forcing technology.xml back into the VIBE core model.
consequences.negative: Maintainers must keep the shim boundary explicit in docs and verification.

review.notes: Applies whenever GRACE tooling is used against a VIBE-core repository.

D-015.summary: Keep the repository root as the clean public VIBE workspace and quarantine internal and legacy surfaces explicitly.

context.problem: After the old vibestart v3 package was quarantined, the repository still needed an explicit root-boundary rule so new product work would not leak back into legacy or internal surfaces.
context.constraints: The public root surface must stay small, agent-agnostic, and releaseable; compatibility artifacts may remain in the repo, but they must stay explicit.

option-1.name: Soft boundary by team habit
option-1.description: Rely on maintainers to remember which surfaces are clean, internal, compatibility-only, or legacy-only.
option-1.cons: Boundary drift returns quickly and archive/release surfaces become ambiguous again.

option-2.name: Explicit clean-root workspace boundary
option-2.description: Define the repository root as the public VIBE workspace, keep internal and legacy surfaces explicit, and exclude them from the clean release archive.
option-2.pros: Creates a stable public working surface and protects future product work from drifting back into quarantined paths.
option-2.cons: Requires repo-level boundary documentation and verification.

decision.rationale: The repository now needs a formal workspace contract, not just a one-time migration move, so future VIBE and vibestart work lands on one public root surface.

consequences.positive: New public work has one explicit home and release packaging becomes more predictable.
consequences.negative: Maintainers must keep README and archive policy aligned with the actual repository layout.

review.notes: Also keeps the compatibility shim and quarantined legacy package from being mistaken for active product surfaces.

D-016.summary: Ship a working root vibestart entrypoint around the shared surface and core behavior before implementing richer deep-specific adapters.

context.problem: After the clean root workspace was established, the repository still lacked an active bootstrap command. Waiting for a fully differentiated deep implementation would delay the first real product path and keep the contract purely documentary.
context.constraints: The working entrypoint must preserve one VIBE methodology, keep profile choice explicit, and avoid copying repository-specific framework XML truth into target projects.

option-1.name: Wait for full deep implementation first
option-1.description: Do not ship an active product entrypoint until deep-specific adapters and richer integration behavior are also implemented.
option-1.cons: Leaves the product contract unproven for longer and delays feedback on the shared install surface.

option-2.name: Implement core-first active bootstrap
option-2.description: Ship a working root vibestart command for the shared install surface and deterministic first-run contract, while keeping deep explicit and safe even if its richer adapters remain future work.
option-2.pros: Creates a usable product path immediately and validates the contract with real execution.
option-2.cons: deep initially differs more by declared product depth than by concrete runtime adapters.

decision.rationale: A working deterministic bootstrap path is more valuable now than waiting for a heavier deep implementation. It proves the shared install surface and first-run contract on real code without compromising the one-methodology rule.

consequences.positive: The repository gets a real active product entrypoint and a safer path for future deep specialization.
consequences.negative: Maintainers still need to implement richer deep adapters later if they want deeper runtime differentiation.

review.notes: Also constrains the generated project surfaces to remain generic project scaffolding instead of copies of framework-repository truth.

D-017.summary: Treat core as the explicit beta boundary now, and close adoption gaps with operator guidance and richer generic scaffolds before promising full legacy GRACE procedural parity.

context.problem: The repository now has strong methodology contracts and one active bootstrap path, but one-project adoption would still lean too heavily on implicit maintainer knowledge or the quarantined GRACE legacy corpus if beta scope and operator guidance stayed vague.
context.constraints: The beta story must keep one VIBE methodology, keep deep explicit without overstating its current richness, and avoid copying framework-repository semantics into project-specific starting artifacts.

option-1.name: Wait for full legacy parity before any beta claim
option-1.description: Delay beta positioning until every detailed GRACE operational mechanic and a richer deep differentiation layer have been fully re-expressed on the clean root surface.
option-1.pros: A more feature-complete future beta message.
option-1.cons: Delays real pilot usage and blocks feedback on the current working core path even though the root bootstrap and contracts already exist.

option-2.name: Declare a core-first beta boundary now
option-2.description: Recommend core as the current beta path, publish VIBE-native operator guidance, and harden generic starting scaffolds so one-project adoption becomes practical now while deeper legacy parity remains future work.
option-2.pros: Keeps the beta claim honest, makes pilot adoption practical, and reduces dependency on the quarantined GRACE package as an active procedure surface.
option-2.cons: Maintainers still need to port or reinvent richer procedural mechanics later if they want a deeper operational layer in the clean root surface.

decision.chosen: Declare a core-first beta boundary now
decision.rationale: The project is strong enough for one real pilot if it clearly says what is beta-ready now and supports that claim with operator guidance and richer generic scaffolds. Waiting for total legacy parity would delay useful feedback without improving the current core path proportionally.

consequences.positive: One-project beta adoption becomes practical now through the clean root surface.
consequences.negative: The team must still port or redesign richer procedural mechanics later if it wants full clean-root operational depth beyond the core beta boundary.

review.notes: Also constrains beta messaging to keep deep explicit but not overclaimed while the richer adapter layer is still future work.

D-018.summary: Make target-repo-first git acquisition the supported prerelease bootstrap path instead of requiring a separate long-lived framework checkout as the main user workflow.

context.problem: The working root bootstrap entrypoint already exists, but the main user story would still force adopters to keep a separate framework checkout around if there were no supported git acquisition wrapper.
context.constraints: The acquisition path must keep git source, ref, profile, and target path explicit, and it must remain a thin wrapper over the existing deterministic bootstrap contract rather than becoming a second methodology surface.

option-1.name: Keep separate local checkout as the main path
option-1.description: Require users to clone or install the framework repo first, then invoke vibestart from that checkout into a target repository.
option-1.cons: Adds friction, weakens the target-repo-first mental model, and makes adoption feel tool-centric instead of project-centric.

option-2.name: Support target-repo-first git acquisition
option-2.description: Let users enter the target repository, fetch vibestart from git, and bootstrap in place through a thin acquisition wrapper.
option-2.pros: Matches the intended adoption UX and keeps the target repository as the active working context.
option-2.cons: Introduces one more entrypoint surface that must stay aligned with the main bootstrap contract.

decision.rationale: The main prerelease bootstrap path should be project-centric. A thin wrapper around the existing bootstrap command is enough to support that path without splitting the product semantics.

consequences.positive: Users can bootstrap directly from inside a target repository using a git source and ref.
consequences.negative: Maintainers must keep the acquisition wrapper aligned with the main bootstrap contract and release docs.

review.notes: Also keeps the acquisition story tied to explicit prerelease refs instead of vague latest-from-main behavior.
